title_patterns: [TICKER/COMPANY]: why are insiders buying [TICKER] stock? — question-form title naming a single verifiable filing event
Insiders just bought $[unrounded dollar total] of these [N] stocks — one stands out (aggregate number + finite list + one implied focal pick)
[N] [category] stock trades you need to see — small odd count (3/5/8) framing a screenable dataset, no directional prediction
[TICKER] stock: the [insider/institutional/filing] move most people missed — 'overlooked data point' framing on a mega-cap name
[EVENT] panel: [TICKER] — event-tagged, ultra-short label title that indexes on the ticker + calendar catalyst
[REGULATOR/INSTITUTION] didn't need [expected gatekeeper]. [Structural change] is now happening. — two-sentence title: fact, then consequence
What actually happened to [index/sector] this week — [N] numbers that explain it (curiosity framed as explanation, not alarm)
[Well-known market figure]'s latest disclosed position — what the filing actually says vs. the headline
hook_patterns: Open with the single hardest number and its source date: 'On [date], [insider/filer] disclosed [exact unrounded amount] in [TICKER]. Here's the filing.' (hypothesis)
State the misconception, then the data correction: 'The headline says X. The actual disclosure says Y — and the difference matters for these three reasons.' (hypothesis)
Scope-and-contract opener: 'I pulled every [filing type] above [threshold] from the last [N] days. Eight qualified. One is unusual — here's the criteria I used.' (hypothesis)
Catalyst timestamp opener: '[Company] reported [N] minutes ago. Three lines from the release actually changed the model — revenue, guidance, and margin.' (hypothesis)
Define the mechanism before the opinion: 'Before the reaction, here's what this rule/filing literally permits — then we'll look at what it doesn't.' (hypothesis)
packaging_notes: Two duration clusters appear: 6–12 min for single-name/single-filing stories and 19–30 min for multi-stock screens or event panels. Sub-3-min list videos exist but function as list-scan content, not analysis.

Insider- and disclosure-driven framing (insider buys, congressional/public-figure filings, institutional moves) recurs across multiple independent channels — it is verifiable-document territory, which fits a no-hype channel better than macro prediction.
Numbers that travel are aggregate totals with a dollar sign and a finite count ('$500M+ of these 8 stocks'). Odd, unrounded counts and totals read as screen output rather than marketing.
Event-tagged titles (earnings panel, post-report reaction) get lift purely from ticker + calendar proximity, so publishing inside hours of a catalyst matters more than title cleverness.

The high-view macro entries in this set lean on vague-alarm framing ('unthinkable', 'WTF'), which is explicitly off-brand here. The transferable structure is the two-part title — declarative fact, then stated consequence — without the emotional adjective.
Question-form titles ('why are insiders buying X?') work when the question is answerable from public data; avoid question titles whose only answer is a forecast.
market_patterns.title: outlier pattern extraction

winning_patterns.pattern: Shorts that pair one ticker's move with a second, contrasting market number (index or volatility move) in the same line
winning_patterns.why_it_holds: The two-number contrast creates an unresolved question (why did this diverge?) that the first seconds can pay off. These titles clustered at hook_hold above 1.10 and 70-89% average view.

winning_patterns.pattern: Named human actor plus a concrete dollar figure, rather than a percentage
winning_patterns.structure: [Company/role] [took a specific action] for [$ amount] + [market context number]
winning_patterns.why_it_holds: Our single highest engaged-view share among mid-view shorts (about 40% of views engaged) and hook_hold above 1.10. A dollar amount with a named decision-maker appears to read as an event, not a price print.

winning_patterns.pattern: Small, precise, unusual counts beat large percentage spikes inside the same franchise
winning_patterns.why_it_holds: Within our social-sentiment franchise, the version built on a rank and a two-digit count retained far better (89% APV, 1.19 hook_hold) than the version built on a three-digit percentage jump in mentions (56% APV, 0.93). Large percentages seem to read as noise; small exact counts read as verifiable.

winning_patterns.pattern: One ticker, one move, one named catalyst, nothing else
winning_patterns.why_it_holds: Tight three-element shorts titles with a specific catalyst noun held above 80% APV even at low view counts, suggesting the viewers who do click stay for the explanation.

winning_patterns.pattern: Reframe/correction structure that denies the obvious read of a move
winning_patterns.why_it_holds: Highest hook_hold values in the set came from titles that set up a contradiction the video resolves. Caveat: both such videos had APV above 100%, which is replay behavior on very low view counts, not proof of demand — treat this as a hook-craft signal only, not a distribution signal.

losing_patterns.pattern: Titles that disclose the caveat and thereby resolve the story before the click
losing_patterns.why_it_hurts: Both of our long videos used a qualifier clause after a dash and both posted the weakest hook_hold in the sample (0.72 and 0.79). If the title already delivers the 'catch,' the first 30% has nothing left to promise.

losing_patterns.pattern: Oversized multipliers and three-to-four-digit percentages as the lead number
losing_patterns.why_it_hurts: Our two most inflated headline numbers had the two lowest hook_hold values among their formats and below-average APV. Extreme numbers appear to trigger skepticism rather than curiosity with this audience.

losing_patterns.pattern: Decline stories loaded with process detail (legal/procedural nouns, clock times)
losing_patterns.why_it_hurts: Lowest APV in the shorts set (51%) with sub-0.9 hook_hold. The second clause adds a new subject the viewer has no stake in, so the hook has to restart.

losing_patterns.pattern: Generic recap suffix appended after the specific hook
losing_patterns.why_it_hurts: The one title carrying a dated recap tag had the lowest views in the set and weak hook_hold. The suffix consumes title real estate with information that dates the video and specifies nothing.

notes: Two shorts show APV above 100% at 47-57 views; that is replay/loop behavior on a tiny base, not evidence of broad demand. Read their hook_hold as craft signal and ignore their APV ranking.
market_close is our volume container, not a hook: it spans 51% to 143% APV. Retention inside it tracks the title's framing (contrast, reframe, named catalyst) far more than the franchise itself.

Only 2 long videos, both with weak hook_hold but unusually high engaged-view share (61% and 77% of views). Long-form is currently reaching a small self-selected audience — don't conclude the title shape failed on distribution from this sample.
